sections.content: Impersonal *se* lets a historical text state a fact or a common practice without naming who does it — useful when the subject is everyone, unknown, or simply beside the point. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: Hoy se suele hablar de 'imperio mexica' aunque, en sentido estricto, gobernaban tres ciudades juntas.
items.english: Today people usually talk about a 'Mexica empire,' though strictly speaking three cities governed together.

items.spanish: Se sabe con gran detalle qué se exigía a cada región gracias al Códice Mendoza.
items.english: It's known in great detail what was demanded of each region, thanks to the Codex Mendoza.

items.spanish: En las chinampas se cultivaban varias cosechas al año.
items.english: On the chinampas, several harvests a year were grown.

items.spanish: Se calcula que casi dos millones de personas hablan náhuatl en México en la actualidad.
items.english: It's estimated that almost two million people speak Nahuatl in Mexico today.

sections.content: Impersonal *se* + third-person singular verb (*se sabe, se calcula, se suele hablar*) works with a verb that has no clear direct object. When there IS a direct object being acted on (*se cultivaban varias cosechas*), the verb agrees with that object instead — this is technically the passive *se*, but in practice historical writing blurs the two constantly.
